basic_information.name: China AI Regulatory Suite (Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions, Deep Synthesis Provisions, Generative AI Interim Measures, AI-Generated Content Labeling Measures, and supplementary standards)
basic_information.effective_date: Phased rollout across multiple regulations: Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions effective 1 March 2022; Deep Synthesis Provisions effective 10 January 2023; Generative AI Interim Measures effective 15 August 2023; AI-Generated Content Labeling Measures (GB 45438-2025) effective 1 September 2025; Generative AI Security Standards effective 1 November 2025; Cybersecurity Law AI amendments effective 1 January 2026; Draft Human-like Interactive AI Measures under public consultation (Dec 2025–Jan 2026)

scope_and_content.summary: China has developed a layered suite of AI regulations rather than a single comprehensive AI law, addressing AI technologies through targeted administrative measures as they emerge. The framework consists of four main enacted regulations — governing algorithmic recommendations (2022), deep synthesis/deepfakes (2023), generative AI services (2023), and AI content labeling (2025) — supplemented by mandatory national security standards, a rapidly growing algorithm filing registry, and AI-specific amendments to the Cybersecurity Law (2026). The approach prioritizes state control over information flows, content alignment with 'socialist core values,' and user protection, while simultaneously promoting domestic AI industry development through the 'AI Plus' Action Plan.
key_provisions: ALGORITHMIC RECOMMENDATION PROVISIONS (March 2022): Internet information service providers using recommendation algorithms must establish algorithm management systems; disclose recommendation service rules; optimize models to present content aligned with 'mainstream value orientation'; give users the right to opt out of personalized recommendations, delete personal characteristics, and avoid price discrimination; prohibit algorithms that induce user addiction or excessive consumption; require licensing for algorithmic recommendation in online news; prohibit algorithmic generation of fake news

DEEP SYNTHESIS PROVISIONS (January 2023): All content created by deep synthesis (deepfake) tools must be labeled as synthetic via watermarks, digital tags, or other visible and invisible markers; providers must ensure file traceability with full data chain compliance; operators must implement content moderation systems; reinforced requirements for especially immersive uses (deepfakes, voice clones, digital avatars); data collection and processing must comply with Personal Information Protection Law principles of legality, necessity, fairness, and transparency; users must obtain express consent from individuals whose biometric data is synthesized

GENERATIVE AI INTERIM MEASURES (August 2023): Generative AI services must align content with socialist core values and not generate content undermining state security, national unity, or social stability; providers must implement human moderation and complaint mechanisms; models and algorithms must be registered with authorities via the CAC algorithm filing system; explicit user consent required for data use; security assessments mandatory for services with public opinion influence; providers must label AI-generated content; training data must comply with data protection requirements including the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and PIPL

AI-GENERATED CONTENT LABELING MEASURES (September 2025): Mandatory explicit labeling (visible text, audio, or graphic indicators) on all AI-generated text, images, audio, video, virtual scenes, and other content; mandatory implicit labeling (digital watermarks or metadata) embedded in files containing service provider name and content identifier; obligations fall on both 'internet information service providers' and 'providers of online content distribution services'; platforms must verify and enforce labeling compliance; accompanied by mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025 specifying technical labeling methods

ALGORITHM FILING REGISTRY: All providers of algorithmic recommendation, deep synthesis, and generative AI services must file with the CAC; as of November 2025, over 5,000 algorithms registered; generative AI applications must display AI model names and filing numbers prominently; registry growing by 250-300 entries monthly; managed through beian.cac.gov.cn platform

CYBERSECURITY LAW AI AMENDMENTS (January 2026): Brings AI explicitly into national law for the first time; Article 20 supports AI fundamental research, algorithm development, and infrastructure construction (training data, computing power); strengthens AI ethical standards and risk monitoring; establishes extraterritorial reach for overseas actors whose activities harm China's cybersecurity; enhanced penalty regime with fines up to RMB 10 million for particularly serious violations

THREE GENERATIVE AI SECURITY STANDARDS (November 2025): National standards specifying basic security requirements for generative AI services including corpus safety, model safety, and safety measures for training data and datasets

DRAFT HUMAN-LIKE INTERACTIVE AI MEASURES (December 2025): Proposed rules for AI products with simulated human personality traits and emotional interaction capabilities; mandatory AI disclosure to users; intervention requirements when extreme emotions or addiction detected; special protections for minors including guardian consent and parental controls; prohibition on obstructing users from exiting emotional companionship services
scope_and_content.risk_classification: China does not use a formal risk-tier classification system like the EU AI Act. Instead, it regulates by technology type and application domain: algorithmic recommendation services face one set of rules, deep synthesis technologies face another, and generative AI services face a third. Within each category, obligations escalate based on potential societal impact — services with 'public opinion influence' face additional security assessment requirements, and 'especially immersive' deep synthesis uses (deepfakes, voice clones) face reinforced labeling and consent obligations. The approach is more technology-specific than risk-tier-based.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: Providers of algorithmic recommendation services, deep synthesis technology services and technical supporters, generative AI service providers, internet information service providers, providers of online content distribution services (platforms), and users/deployers. The Generative AI Interim Measures exclude R&D and internal use from compliance obligations. The Cybersecurity Law amendments also cover overseas organizations and individuals engaging in activities that harm China's cybersecurity.
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Horizontal application across all sectors where covered technologies are deployed. The AI Plus Action Plan specifically targets AI integration in six priority areas: science and technology, industrial utilization, consumer services, public welfare, governance and security, and international collaboration. Online news services face additional licensing requirements for algorithmic recommendation. The Cybersecurity Law provides heightened obligations for critical information infrastructure (CII) operators across energy, transport, finance, public services, e-government, and other key sectors.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: China's AI regulations do not provide explicit open-source exemptions comparable to the EU AI Act. The Generative AI Interim Measures apply to all providers of public-facing generative AI services regardless of whether the underlying model is open-source or proprietary. However, the R&D exemption (excluding research and internal use from compliance obligations) effectively reduces the regulatory burden on open-source model developers during the development phase. China's 'AI Plus' Action Plan (August 2025) explicitly encourages the open-source ecosystem as one of the technical foundations for AI development, and the State Council has promoted open-source sharing and cross-sector data cooperation. In practice, open-source models like DeepSeek have filed with the CAC registry and comply with the same obligations as proprietary models when offered as public services.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: Limited extraterritorial reach under the original AI-specific regulations, which primarily target service providers operating within China. However, the October 2025 Cybersecurity Law amendments significantly expand extraterritorial scope: the revised CSL now covers any overseas organizations and individuals engaging in activities that harm China's cybersecurity (previously limited to activities harming critical information infrastructure). Enforcement powers include pursuing legal liability against overseas actors and, for serious consequences, the Public Security department may freeze assets or impose other necessary measures. Article 20 of the Generative AI Interim Measures also empowers the CAC to take 'technical measures and other necessary actions' to block Chinese users' access to non-compliant foreign services. The CASS Model AI Law draft proposes further extraterritorial application to any AI activities outside China that affect China's national security, public interests, or the rights of individuals/organizations in China.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: Penalty regimes vary across regulations and have been significantly strengthened by the 2025 Cybersecurity Law amendments. GENERATIVE AI INTERIM MEASURES: Article 21 provides relatively mild sanctions — warnings, notifications, criticisms, corrective actions, and suspension of services; notably, the final version removed all references to specific fines and service termination that were in the draft. DEEP SYNTHESIS PROVISIONS: Non-compliance can lead to investigations by regulators, administrative fines on both companies and responsible individuals, business suspension, and criminal liability for serious violations. CYBERSECURITY LAW (effective Jan 2026): Substantially increased fines — first-time violations RMB 10,000–50,000; uncorrected violations RMB 50,000–500,000; violations causing harm up to RMB 1 million for CII impacts; particularly serious consequences up to RMB 10 million (circa USD 1.4 million) for businesses and RMB 1 million (circa USD 140,000) for responsible individuals; selling non-compliant products with illegal gains over RMB 100,000 faces fines of 1–5x the illegal gains. GENERAL: Article 20 of the Generative AI Measures empowers CAC to block foreign services from Chinese users. Up to 5% of annual revenue fines possible under broader regulatory framework.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: Multi-agency enforcement model with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) holding overall coordination authority. Co-regulators include: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), Ministry of Public Security (MPS), State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR), Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST), and National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC). The CAC jointly issued the Deep Synthesis Provisions with MIIT and MPS; the Generative AI Interim Measures with seven agencies total. Local cyberspace and public security departments handle enforcement within their administrative regions.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Staggered across multiple years: March 2022 — Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions in force; January 2023 — Deep Synthesis Provisions in force; August 2023 — Generative AI Interim Measures in force; September 2025 — AI-Generated Content Labeling Measures and mandatory standard GB 45438-2025 in force; November 2025 — Three national Generative AI Security Standards in force; January 2026 — Cybersecurity Law AI amendments in force; ongoing — Human-like Interactive AI Measures under public consultation (Dec 2025–Jan 2026), expected finalization in 2026. A comprehensive omnibus AI law was removed from the 2025 legislative agenda, but NPC representatives continue proposing its drafting; state media signal it remains on the horizon.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: ALGORITHM FILING: All providers of algorithmic recommendation, deep synthesis, and generative AI services must register algorithms with the CAC via beian.cac.gov.cn, including model names, filing numbers, and technical details; these must be displayed prominently in products. SECURITY ASSESSMENTS: Services with 'public opinion influence' must undergo security assessments per Article 17 of the Generative AI Measures. CONTENT LABELING: All AI-generated content must carry both explicit (visible) and implicit (watermark/metadata) labels per the September 2025 Labeling Measures. INSPECTION COOPERATION: Article 19 of the Generative AI Measures requires providers to cooperate fully with inspections by officials and provide transparency. INCIDENT REPORTING: The Cybersecurity Law amendments strengthen incident reporting obligations for cybersecurity events. CONTENT MODERATION: Providers must implement human moderation, accessible complaint systems, and maintain records of content generation and user interactions.
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: China's AI regulations do not include specific SME exemptions, reduced documentation, or sandbox access provisions comparable to the EU AI Act. However, the regulatory approach provides de facto relief for smaller players through several mechanisms: (1) the Generative AI Interim Measures exempt R&D and internal use from compliance, reducing burden on companies still in development phase; (2) the deliberate decision to remove comprehensive AI legislation from the 2025 agenda was partly motivated by keeping compliance costs low; (3) the AI Plus Action Plan encourages business participation and cross-sector AI adoption without distinguishing by company size; (4) the algorithm filing process is administrative rather than costly; (5) local governments operate AI development zones and pilot programs that provide support for smaller companies. In practice, China's enforcement has focused primarily on large platforms (WeChat, Douyin, Weibo) rather than smaller startups. Nevertheless, the absence of formal SME provisions means smaller companies face the same legal obligations as large enterprises.
compliance_and_enforcement.liability_model: fault_based (primary). China's Civil Code provides three types of tortious liability (fault-based, fault with presumption, strict liability). For generative AI services specifically, fault-based liability applies rather than strict liability, reflecting a policy choice to encourage AI development. Courts determine fault by examining whether providers fulfilled their duty of care: compliance with regulatory obligations (algorithm filing, complaint mechanisms, risk disclosure, content labeling), adoption of appropriate preventive measures, and adherence to content moderation requirements. If an AI service were classified as a 'product,' strict product liability could apply, but current regulatory framing treats generative AI as services rather than products. The CASS Model AI Law draft proposes more structured liability provisions, but these remain at the academic proposal stage.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: LARGE ENTERPRISES: Major domestic tech companies (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance) have integrated compliance as a core function, filing algorithms with the CAC, implementing content moderation systems, and deploying AI labeling on platforms like WeChat, Douyin, and Weibo. The compliance infrastructure doubles as a competitive moat against smaller competitors and foreign entrants. Companies preparing for IPOs must demonstrate algorithm review systems, data security protocols, and age-verification mechanisms. STARTUPS AND SMEs: Face contradictory pressures — on one hand, the regulatory framework's focus on public-facing services and the R&D exemption provides breathing room during development; on the other hand, once launching public services, startups face the same filing, moderation, and labeling obligations as large enterprises without proportionate cost relief. The fragmented regulatory landscape (four separate regulations plus standards) increases compliance complexity. Chinese AI startups, particularly in the emotional companion space (e.g., Minimax's Talkie, Zhipu), face new operational hurdles from the December 2025 draft Human-like AI measures. FOREIGN COMPANIES: Effectively locked out of China's consumer AI market — the combination of content alignment requirements ('socialist core values'), algorithm filing, and CAC inspection powers makes foreign generative AI service provision practically impossible. Foreign companies developing AI for global markets face potential extraterritorial reach under the amended Cybersecurity Law if their activities are deemed to harm China's cybersecurity. POSITIVE EFFECTS: The AI Plus Action Plan (August 2025) sets ambitious targets for AI adoption — 70% penetration in key sectors by 2027, 90% by 2030 — creating massive market opportunities for compliant AI providers of all sizes.
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: China's regulatory approach deliberately balances state control with innovation promotion, producing a complex and sometimes contradictory effect. PROMOTING INNOVATION: (1) The R&D exemption in the Generative AI Measures shields research from compliance burden; (2) The AI Plus Action Plan commits to strengthening technical foundations — models, algorithms, high-quality data, computing power, talent, and open-source ecosystem; (3) The State Council has set aggressive AI adoption targets through 2035; (4) Algorithm filing has been made relatively light-touch (administrative rather than technically burdensome); (5) The deliberate delay of comprehensive omnibus legislation preserves regulatory flexibility. CONSTRAINING INNOVATION: (1) Content alignment requirements ('socialist core values,' prohibition of content undermining state security) significantly constrain what AI systems can generate and recommend; (2) The fragmented regulatory landscape creates uncertainty for businesses navigating overlapping obligations; (3) Content moderation and human review requirements add operational costs; (4) The labeling obligations (visible + watermark) add technical implementation burden; (5) Blocking of foreign AI services (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) limits exposure to competitive benchmarks for some use cases. NET ASSESSMENT: Domestic AI development has thrived under the framework — 346 generative AI services filed by March 2025, over 5,000 algorithms registered by November 2025, and breakthrough models like DeepSeek emerged. The constraints primarily affect content and expression rather than technical capability.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: China's AI regulatory model exerts influence through several channels but differs fundamentally from the EU's 'Brussels effect.' DIRECT INFLUENCE: (1) China published a 'Global AI Governance Action Plan' (July 2025) positioning itself as a global AI governance leader; (2) The technology-specific regulatory approach (rather than risk-tier) has influenced some developing countries' thinking; (3) China's content labeling standards (GB 45438-2025) are among the most technically detailed globally; (4) The algorithm filing registry is the world's largest and most comprehensive, with no equivalent elsewhere. DISTINCTIVE MODEL: China's regulatory philosophy emphasizes state control, content alignment, and social stability rather than individual rights or market competition, making it a genuinely alternative model to both the EU's rights-based approach and the US's innovation-first approach. This 'third way' appeals to some authoritarian and semi-authoritarian governments. LIMITATIONS: (1) The content alignment requirements are specific to China's political system and not exportable; (2) The extraterritorial enforcement mechanisms are weaker than the EU's market-access leverage; (3) Western democracies are unlikely to adopt the state-control model. STANDARDS COMPETITION: China is actively working to shape international AI standards through the ITU and ISO processes, and its technical standards on labeling and security may influence global norms even where its governance philosophy does not.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: GOVERNMENT/PARTY: Views AI as both a national competitiveness imperative and an information control challenge. The party's primary concerns include: maintaining control over the information environment, managing socioeconomic impacts of AI on work and education, and preventing AI from escaping human (and party) control. The removal of omnibus AI legislation from the 2025 agenda reflects a pragmatic decision to maintain flexibility while the technology evolves rapidly. DOMESTIC INDUSTRY: Major tech companies (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei) have participated actively in governance framework development through government-adjacent technical organizations and contributed to standards development. Industry generally supports the regulatory framework as providing market certainty while keeping obligations manageable. Companies benefit from the de facto barrier to foreign competition. ACADEMIA: The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) has led development of expert draft proposals for a comprehensive AI Law (Model AI Law, with version 2.0 released April 2025), reflecting scholarly consensus on the need for higher-level legislation. Leading universities and research labs contributed to the governance framework. CIVIL SOCIETY: Extremely limited voice in China's regulatory process. Research indicates Chinese public concerns center on eight AI ethics dimensions: safety, transparency, fairness, personal data protection, liability, truthfulness, human autonomy, and human dignity. China ranks last among major AI powers in policies protecting freedom of expression in AI (per Lawfare analysis). INTERNATIONAL OBSERVERS: Carnegie Endowment and other Western think tanks note that China's regulations reflect genuine risk management alongside information control objectives; some observers see China's approach as more pragmatic and technology-responsive than the EU's.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: China is not deregulating AI but is deliberately pacing its regulatory ambitions. KEY SIGNALS: (1) The comprehensive AI law was removed from the 2025 NPC legislative agenda, with officials instead prioritizing 'pilots, standards, and targeted rules' — this represents a pause in horizontal regulation, not a retreat; (2) The Generative AI Interim Measures deliberately softened penalties compared to the draft version, removing fines and service termination provisions; (3) The AI Plus Action Plan (August 2025) signals a strong pro-development orientation with targets of 70% AI penetration by 2027; (4) The State Council's language emphasizes 'healthy development' and 'encouraging innovation' alongside 'managing risks.' COUNTER-SIGNALS: (1) The Cybersecurity Law amendments (Jan 2026) significantly strengthen penalties and expand extraterritorial reach; (2) New regulations continue to be issued at a rapid pace (labeling rules, security standards, human-like AI draft); (3) The algorithm filing registry continues to grow rapidly with increasing mandatory compliance. NET ASSESSMENT: China is pursuing a dual-track strategy — promoting AI development and adoption aggressively while maintaining tight content and information controls. The 'deregulatory' signals are better understood as strategic regulatory pacing rather than genuine deregulation.

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: Critical case study for understanding alternative AI governance models and market access strategies. KEY IMPLICATIONS: (1) MARKET ACCESS BARRIER — China's content alignment requirements ('socialist core values'), algorithm filing, and CAC inspection powers create a near-impenetrable barrier for foreign AI service providers; European AI startups targeting the Chinese market must understand that the regulatory framework effectively mandates domestic partnerships or local entity establishment; (2) REGULATORY SPEED — China's ability to issue targeted regulations within months of technology emergence (deep synthesis rules within a year of deepfake proliferation, generative AI rules within months of ChatGPT launch) contrasts sharply with the EU's multi-year legislative process, offering lessons in regulatory agility; (3) COMPLIANCE-AS-COMPETITIVE-MOAT — for Chinese AI companies, early compliance with filing and labeling requirements creates barriers to entry; the same dynamic applies globally — companies that master multi-jurisdictional compliance (EU + China + US) gain significant competitive advantage; (4) DUAL-TRACK MODEL — China's simultaneous pursuit of aggressive AI promotion (70% penetration by 2027) and strict content control illustrates how regulatory philosophy shapes market structure; entrepreneurs must recognize that 'AI-friendly regulation' can coexist with tight content restrictions; (5) LABELING TECHNOLOGY MARKET — China's mandatory technical labeling requirements (visible + watermark) create a market for AI content detection and labeling tools that parallels the EU's transparency requirements; (6) CONTENT MODERATION INFRASTRUCTURE — the requirement for human moderation and complaint systems means every AI deployment requires compliance infrastructure, creating business opportunities in compliance-as-a-service; (7) COMPARATIVE REGULATION ANALYSIS — comparing China's technology-specific approach with the EU's risk-tier approach and the US's sector-specific patchwork helps entrepreneurs understand which regulatory model best supports their business strategy and which markets to prioritize.
teaching_relevance.session_mapping: Session 5 (Ethics, governance & final presentations) — primary session for comparing China's state-control model with EU and US approaches. Also relevant to Session 1 (Fundamentals & AI landscape) for understanding the global AI ecosystem's regulatory fragmentation, and Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) for analyzing how regulatory environments shape market entry strategies and competitive dynamics.

confidence.data_quality: High — based on official regulatory texts translated by authoritative sources (ChinaLawTranslate, DigiChina/Stanford), analysis from major international law firms (White & Case, Mayer Brown, Bird & Bird, Linklaters, Loeb & Loeb, Reed Smith, DLA Piper, Latham & Watkins), CSET Georgetown translations of official Chinese government publications, and reporting from official Chinese media (CGTN, Global Times, Legal Daily). Filing statistics from official CAC announcements and SCIO press conferences.
confidence.cross_reference: ChinaLawTranslate.com (full regulatory text translations), DigiChina at Stanford University, CSET Georgetown University, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, IAPP Global AI Governance tracker, Chambers and Partners Artificial Intelligence 2025 China guide, Global Legal Insights AI 2025 China chapter, White & Case AI Watch China tracker, Lawfare, East Asia Forum, China Briefing. Filing registry statistics cross-referenced between SCIO press conferences, CAC official data, and Gradient Flow analysis.
confidence.caveats: The regulatory landscape is evolving extremely rapidly: (1) A comprehensive omnibus AI law remains expected but has been deferred — when enacted, it could restructure the entire regulatory framework; (2) The Human-like Interactive AI Measures were in draft as of December 2025, with final provisions potentially differing from the consultation draft; (3) Penalty enforcement practices may differ from statutory provisions — China's enforcement has focused on large platforms, and actual penalty amounts and frequency for AI-specific violations remain limited in public reporting; (4) The CASS Model AI Law is an academic proposal without official status but may heavily influence eventual comprehensive legislation; (5) International sanctions and chip export controls affecting China's AI hardware access could drive further regulatory adjustments; (6) The Generative AI Interim Measures' title ('interim') explicitly signals they are intended as a temporary framework pending more comprehensive legislation; (7) Translation nuances — English translations of Chinese regulatory texts may not fully capture legal precision, especially around terms like 'socialist core values' and 'mainstream value orientation.'
